```{r setup, include=FALSE}
options(repos = c(CRAN = "https://cloud.r-project.org"))
for (p in c("tidyverse", "knitr", "effsize", "lme4", "mediation")) if (!require(p, character.only = TRUE)) install.packages(p)
library(tidyverse); library(knitr); library(effsize); library(lme4); library(mediation)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
# kable with two-line headers: an x_y column name is shown as x over y (LaTeX \shortstack; a space in HTML)
tbl <- function(df, ...) {
  if (knitr::is_latex_output()) {
    names(df) <- ifelse(grepl("_", names(df)), sprintf("\\shortstack{%s}", gsub("_", "\\\\\\\\", names(df))), names(df))
    df[] <- lapply(df, function(x) if (is.character(x) || is.factor(x)) gsub("_", "\\\\_", as.character(x)) else x)
    kable(df, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, longtable = TRUE, linesep = "", escape = FALSE, ...)   # real LaTeX table: columns size to content, stays in place, no row gaps
  } else { names(df) <- gsub("_", " ", names(df)); kable(df, ...) }
}
set.seed(1)
```

This document contains the three contextualization analyses of Section III-A3:
whether the 52 study postconditions are balanced between correct and incorrect
(Part 1), how they compare with six external corpora (Part 2), and how the 26
functions compare with the rest of HumanEval and with real-world methods (Part 3).

# Part 1: Balance of correct and incorrect postconditions

## Overview

We show that the correct and incorrect postconditions do not differ significantly
in complexity, and that postcondition complexity does not explain the effect of 
correctness on participant accuracy: adding any complexity metric to the accuracy 
model leaves the correctness effect unchanged, and no metric carries an indirect 
(mediated) effect.

```{r}
lt <- read.csv("../data/quant_longtable.csv") %>%
  rename(Cyclomatic = Cyclomatic_Complexity_Postcondition,
         Cognitive = Cognitive_Complexity_Postcondition,
         Halstead_Difficulty = Halstead_Difficulty_Postcondition)

sm_metrics <- c("OperatorCount", "OperatorNesting", "DistinctOperatorCount",
                "NegationCount", "NegationLevel", "NegationNesting",
                "AndCount", "OrCount", "ImplicationCount", "ImplicationNesting",
                "IffCount", "SM_Score")

classic_metrics <- c("Cognitive", "Cyclomatic", "Halstead_Difficulty")
all_metrics <- c(classic_metrics, sm_metrics)
smaller_metrics_set <- c("Cognitive", "Cyclomatic", "Halstead_Difficulty",
                         "SM_Score")

metrics_accuracy <- lt %>%
  group_by(Function_Seen, Postcondition_Correct) %>%
  summarise(n_shown = n(), accuracy = mean(Participant_Correct),
            across(c(Postcondition_Seen, SM_Formula, all_of(all_metrics)), first), .groups = "drop")

cat("Responses:", nrow(lt), " Participants:", n_distinct(lt$Pid),
    " Functions:", n_distinct(lt$Function_Seen), " Postconditions:", nrow(metrics_accuracy), "\n")
```

## 2. Postconditions are Balanced in Complexity

No metric differs significantly across the 26 function-matched postcondition
pairs (paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests on cyclomatic, cognitive and Halstead
complexity and on all Shevrin & Maoz properties and their score). 
The mean within-pair difference is at most 0.21 standard deviations. For some 
metrics, correct postconditions have higher complexities, and for others,
incorrect postconditions have higher complexities.
```{r}
incorrect <- metrics_accuracy %>% filter(Postcondition_Correct == 0) %>% 
  arrange(Function_Seen)
correct   <- metrics_accuracy %>% filter(Postcondition_Correct == 1) %>% 
  arrange(Function_Seen)

balance_table <- function(metrics) map_dfr(metrics, function(m) {
  tibble(metric = m,
         med_incorrect = median(incorrect[[m]]), med_correct = median(correct[[m]]),
         mean_incorrect = mean(incorrect[[m]]),  mean_correct = mean(correct[[m]]),
         mean_diff = mean(incorrect[[m]] - correct[[m]]),
         diff_in_SD = mean(incorrect[[m]] - correct[[m]]) / sd(metrics_accuracy[[m]]),
         p_val = wilcox.test(incorrect[[m]], correct[[m]], paired = TRUE, exact = FALSE)$p.value)
})
construction <- balance_table(all_metrics)
tbl(construction, digits = 2, caption = "Construction: correct and incorrect
postconditions do not differ significantly in complexity across functions")
```

## 2a. Balance in Complexity, shorter table 

Same table as above without the full list of Shevrin & Maoz metrics
```{r}
tbl(balance_table(smaller_metrics_set), digits = 2, caption = "Construction: 
correct and incorrect postconditions do not differ significantly in complexity 
across functions")

```

## 3. Robustness: postcondition complexity does not explain the accuracy effect

### Complexity scores do not predict accuracy:
In the final section of this  comparison, we show that no complexity measures 
improve our participant correctness prediction model and no complexity measures 
mediate the difference we observed in developer ability to correctly identify 
correct versus incorrect postconditions. Adding a complexity metric to the 
accuracy model does not significantly improve fit, minimally changes the OR 
effect of correctness, and has minimal (and not significant, p>0.10 for all) 
mediated effect on participant accuracy.
```{r}

fit <- function(f) glmer(f, data = lt, family = binomial, 
                         control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))
m0 <- fit(Participant_Correct ~ Postcondition_Correct + (1 | Pid) + 
            (1 | Postcondition_Seen))
models <- list(
  "+ Cyclomatic" = fit(Participant_Correct ~ Postcondition_Correct + 
                                   scale(Cyclomatic) + (1 | Pid) + 
                                   (1 | Postcondition_Seen)),
  "+ Cognitive" = fit(Participant_Correct ~ Postcondition_Correct + 
                                   scale(Cognitive) + (1 | Pid) + 
                                   (1 | Postcondition_Seen)),
  "+ Halstead difficulty" = fit(Participant_Correct ~ Postcondition_Correct + 
                                   scale(Halstead_Difficulty) + (1 | Pid) + 
                                   (1 | Postcondition_Seen)),
  "+ Shevrin & Maoz score" = fit(Participant_Correct ~ Postcondition_Correct + 
                                   scale(SM_Score) + (1 | Pid) + 
                                   (1 | Postcondition_Seen))
)

set.seed(0)
mediations <- list(
  mediation::mediate(lm(Cyclomatic ~ Postcondition_Correct, metrics_accuracy),
                     lm(accuracy ~ Postcondition_Correct + Cyclomatic, 
                        metrics_accuracy),
                     treat = "Postcondition_Correct", mediator = "Cyclomatic", 
                     boot = TRUE, sims = 1000),
  mediation::mediate(lm(Cognitive ~ Postcondition_Correct, metrics_accuracy),
                     lm(accuracy ~ Postcondition_Correct + Cognitive, 
                        metrics_accuracy),
                     treat = "Postcondition_Correct", mediator = "Cognitive", 
                     boot = TRUE, sims = 1000),
  mediation::mediate(lm(Halstead_Difficulty ~ Postcondition_Correct, 
                        metrics_accuracy),
                     lm(accuracy ~ Postcondition_Correct + Halstead_Difficulty, 
                        metrics_accuracy),
                     treat = "Postcondition_Correct", mediator = 
                       "Halstead_Difficulty", boot = TRUE, sims = 1000),
  mediation::mediate(lm(SM_Score ~ Postcondition_Correct, metrics_accuracy),
                     lm(accuracy ~ Postcondition_Correct + SM_Score, 
                        metrics_accuracy),
                     treat = "Postcondition_Correct", mediator = "SM_Score", 
                     boot = TRUE, sims = 1000)
)   


correctness_or <- function(m) exp(fixef(m)["Postcondition_Correct"])
model_table <- rbind(
  data.frame(Model = "Base (correctness only)", AIC = AIC(m0), BIC = BIC(m0), 
             LRT_p = NA, Correctness_OR = correctness_or(m0),
             Indirect_effect = NA, Indirect_p = NA),
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(models), function(i) {
    m <- models[[i]]; med <- mediations[[i]]
    data.frame(Model = names(models)[i], AIC = AIC(m), BIC = BIC(m), 
               LRT_p = anova(m0, m)$"Pr(>Chisq)"[2],
               Correctness_OR = correctness_or(m), Indirect_effect = med$d.avg,
               Indirect_p = med$d.avg.p)
  }))
)
rownames(model_table) <- NULL
kable(model_table, digits = c(0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 2),
      col.names = c("Model", "AIC", "BIC", "LRT p", "Correctness OR", 
                    "Mediated effect", "Mediation p"),
      caption = "Adding a complexity metric to the accuracy model does not 
      significantly improve fit, minimally changes the OR effect of correctness,
      has minimal mediated effect")
```


# Part 2: Postcondition representativeness

## Overview

Among postconditions with Boolean structure, our 52 stimuli are statistically 
indistinguishable from PostCondBench's expert refined real world
postconditions (Python: our median at their 57th percentile, Cliff's delta 0.01,
p = 0.93; Java: 64th percentile, delta 0.07, p = 0.41) and from nl2postcond's
Python postconditions (59th, delta 0.13, p = 0.106), and modestly above the
remaining three corpora (72nd to 77th percentile, delta 0.17 to 0.26). Our set
contains fewer single predicate postconditions than any corpus (8% against 24%
to 74%), partly by construction.

We compare against six external corpora using the reading complexity score of
Shevrin and Maoz (TOSEM 2025) and, for the two Python corpora, the three code
complexity metrics as well. Comparisons are rank based throughout: the percentile
of our median within each corpus, Cliff's delta, and a rank sum test.

```{r}
corpora <- read.csv("../data/postcondition_corpora.csv")
study <- corpora %>% filter(dataset == "study")
stopifnot(nrow(study) == 52, !any(is.na(study$SM_Score)))
table(corpora$dataset)

# Per source: number of postconditions, median and mean reading-complexity score, 
# and the share whose formula is a single predicate (p1), which the score 
# cannot rank and which we can't check for non-triviality
corpora %>%
  group_by(dataset) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), median_score = median(SM_Score), mean_score = mean(SM_Score),
            single_predicate = mean(OperatorCount == 0)) %>%
  tbl(digits = 2, caption = "Reading-complexity score by source: median, mean, 
        and share of single-predicate postconditions")

compare <- function(corpus, metric) { 
  keep <- corpora$OperatorCount > 0
  a <- study[[metric]][study$OperatorCount > 0]
  b <- corpora[[metric]][corpora$dataset == corpus & keep]
  data.frame(corpus, metric, n = length(b), study_med = median(a), 
             corpus_med = median(b),
             study_med_prcnt = ecdf(b)(median(a)) * 100,
             p = wilcox.test(a, b)$p.value, 
             cliffs_delta = cliff.delta(a, b)$estimate)
}
p_text <- function(p) ifelse(p < 0.001, "< 0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p))    
```

## Structured postconditions

A single predicate postcondition always receives the same base score, so
the score cannot rank the portion of each corpus that consists of single
predicates (4/52 of our stimuli, which were filtered for logical triviality).
We also have no consistent way of filtering out trivial postconditions from 
this single-predicate set (we did our stimulus filtering manually). 
The comparison below therefore uses only 
postconditions with at least one connective.
```{r}
rbind(compare("postcondbench_py", "SM_Score"),
      compare("postcondbench_java", "SM_Score"),
      compare("nl2postcond_py", "SM_Score"),
      compare("nl2postcond_java", "SM_Score"),
      compare("dafnybench", "SM_Score"),
      compare("jdk_jml", "SM_Score")) %>%
  mutate(p = p_text(p), across(c(study_med, corpus_med), ~ 
                                 sprintf("%.2f", .x))) %>%
  tbl(digits = 2, caption = "Structured postconditions only: where our median 
        falls among each corpus (percentile), Cliff's delta, rank-sum p")
```

```{r fig.height=4, fig.width=8}
all_corpora <- c("study", "nl2postcond_py", "nl2postcond_java", 
                 "postcondbench_py", "postcondbench_java", "dafnybench", 
                 "jdk_jml")
structured <- corpora %>%
  filter(OperatorCount > 0) %>%
  mutate(dataset = factor(dataset, levels = rev(all_corpora)),   
         SM_Score = pmin(SM_Score, quantile(SM_Score, 0.99)))   
p <- ggplot(structured, aes(x = SM_Score, y = dataset, 
                            fill = dataset == "study")) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.6, outlier.alpha = 0.3, width = 0.6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#c9a227", `FALSE` = "grey85"), 
                    guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Reading-complexity score", y = NULL) +
  expand_limits(x = 0) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
p
```

## Python corpora: structured set
```{r}
python <- corpora %>% filter(dataset %in% c("study", "nl2postcond_py", 
                                            "postcondbench_py"), 
                                            OperatorCount > 0)   

rbind(compare("nl2postcond_py", "Cognitive"),
      compare("nl2postcond_py", "Cyclomatic"),
      compare("nl2postcond_py", "Halstead_Difficulty"),
      compare("postcondbench_py", "Cognitive"),
      compare("postcondbench_py", "Cyclomatic"),
      compare("postcondbench_py", "Halstead_Difficulty"))%>%
  mutate(p = p_text(p), across(c(study_med, corpus_med), ~ 
                                 sprintf("%.2f", .x))) %>%
  tbl(digits = 2, caption = "Structured postconditions only: study vs. the 
        Python corpora on each complexity metric")
```

```{r fig.height=4, fig.width=8}
python_metrics <- c("Cognitive", "Cyclomatic", "Halstead_Difficulty")   
python_long <- python %>%
  dplyr::select(dataset, all_of(python_metrics)) %>%     
  pivot_longer(-dataset, names_to = "metric") %>%
  mutate(metric = factor(metric, levels = python_metrics),
         dataset = factor(dataset, levels = c("postcondbench_py", 
                                              "nl2postcond_py", "study"))) %>%  
  group_by(metric) %>%
  mutate(value = pmin(value, quantile(value, 0.99))) %>%  
  ungroup()
p <- ggplot(python_long, aes(x = value, y = dataset, fill = dataset == "study")) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.6, outlier.alpha = 0.3, width = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ metric, scales = "free_x", ncol = 3) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#c9a227", `FALSE` = "grey85"), guide = "none") +
  expand_limits(x = 0) +                                   # every panel's axis starts at zero
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
p
```


# Part 3: Function representativeness

## Overview

We show that our 26 functions are representative of HumanEval and contextualize 
against Postcondbench

```{r}
functions <- read.csv("../data/function_metrics.csv")
functions$used <- as.logical(toupper(functions$used))   
functions$group <- ifelse(functions$source == "postcondbench", "PostCondBench (210)",
                   ifelse(functions$used, "Survey (26)", "HumanEval (138)"))
humaneval <- functions %>% filter(source == "humaneval")
used <- functions %>% filter(used)
rest <- functions %>% filter(source == "humaneval", !used)
realworld <- functions %>% filter(source == "postcondbench")

# The 26 vs. one other group on one metric: medians, Cliff's delta with 95% CI
# (positive = the 26 are larger), rank-sum p.
compare <- function(metric, other) {
  a <- used[[metric]]; b <- other[[metric]]
  d <- cliff.delta(a, b)
  data.frame(metric, med_used = median(a), med_other = median(b),
             used_med_prcnt = ecdf(b)(median(a)) * 100,         
             cliffs_delta = d$estimate, ci_low = d$conf.int[1], 
             ci_high = d$conf.int[2],
             p = wilcox.test(a, b)$p.value, row.names = NULL)
}
p_text <- function(p) ifelse(p < 0.001, "< 0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p))    
```

## 1. The 26 functions within HumanEval

Our 26 function-level stimuli did not differ significantly from the rest of 
HumanEval on cognitive complexity, Halstead difficulty or lines of code, and the 
observed effect sizes are negligible (Cliff's delta 0.01 to 0.14). On cyclomatic 
complexity they are slightly more complex (delta = 0.24, p = 0.046).

```{r}

rbind(compare("cognitive", rest),
      compare("cyclomatic", rest),
      compare("halstead_difficulty", rest),
      compare("sloc", rest)) %>%
  mutate(p = p_text(p)) %>%
  tbl(digits = 2, caption = "The 26 functions vs. the other 138 HumanEval 
        problems")

# where the 26 fall within all of HumanEval on cyclomatic complexity 
# (percentiles of min, median, max)
ecdf(humaneval$cyclomatic)(c(min(used$cyclomatic), median(used$cyclomatic), 
                             max(used$cyclomatic)))
```

## 2. The 26 functions against real-world methods

On cyclomatic complexity the 26 functions are close to these methods 
(median 4 vs 5, p = 0.062, our median
at their 47th percentile); on cognitive complexity, which also counts
nesting, they are simpler (median 3 vs 5, p = 0.006); on Halstead difficulty
they do not significantly differ (p = 0.121); and they are shorter 
(median 6.5 vs 13 lines, p < 0.001).
```{r}

rbind(compare("cognitive", realworld),
      compare("cyclomatic", realworld),
      compare("halstead_difficulty", realworld),
      compare("sloc", realworld)) %>%
  mutate(p = p_text(p)) %>%
  tbl(digits = 2, caption = "The 26 functions vs. 210 real-world Python 
        methods")

```

```{r fig.height=4, fig.width=8}
## Box plots of the function-level metrics for the three groups.
metrics <- c("cognitive", "cyclomatic", "halstead_difficulty", "sloc")
functions_long <- functions %>%
  mutate(group = factor(group, levels = c("PostCondBench (210)", 
                                          "HumanEval (138)", "Survey (26)"))) %>%  
  dplyr::select(group, all_of(metrics)) %>%    
  pivot_longer(-group, names_to = "metric") %>%
  mutate(metric = dplyr::recode(metric, cyclomatic = "Cyclomatic complexity", 
                                cognitive = "Cognitive complexity",
                         halstead_difficulty = "Halstead difficulty", 
                         sloc = "Source lines"))

p <- ggplot(functions_long, aes(x = value, y = group, 
                                fill = group == "Survey (26)")) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.6, outlier.alpha = 0.4, width = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ metric, scales = "free_x", ncol = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#c9a227", `FALSE` = "grey85"), 
                    guide = "none") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
p
```
